explanations.explanation: Yes, and it says so right up front: “Then the LORD raised up against Solomon an adversary, Hadad the Edomite, from the royal line of Edom.” Solomon is David's son and Israel's king, and this is the first of the troublemakers on the list. The text gives the LORD as the one who raised him up, so we leave it right there. We don't need to add anything to it.

Verse 14 says it plainly: “Then the LORD raised up against Solomon an adversary, Hadad the Edomite…” Solomon, David's son and Israel's king, didn't stumble into this one. Hadad comes from the royal line of Edom, and the LORD is the one who raised him up. So this statement is true, friend, and the text backs it up.

explanations.answer: He fled the country as a young boy
explanations.explanation: That's it. Verse 17 says Hadad was “still just a young boy” when he fled to Egypt, along with some Edomites who were servants of his father. Joab, the army's commander, did his sweep of Edom, and Hadad was already gone. Small boy, long road, and he lived to come back as trouble for Solomon.

explanations.answer: Joab spared him as a royal prisoner
explanations.explanation: Good thinking, but the text never says Joab caught him or kept him. Verse 17 says Hadad, “still just a young boy,” had fled to Egypt, along with some Edomites who were servants of his father. Joab never got his hands on him. Hadad got out first.

explanations.answer: He was away on a trip to Tyre
explanations.explanation: Tyre never shows up in this story, friend. The text says Hadad, “still just a young boy,” had fled to Egypt, along with some Edomites who were servants of his father. It wasn't a trip. He ran, and he ran with company.

Egypt is right. Verse 17 says Hadad fled to Egypt along with some Edomites who were servants of his father. They didn't go straight there, either. They set out from Midian and went to Paran before reaching Pharaoh, king of Egypt (1 Kings 11:18).

Moab is a fair guess, since it's another neighbor in this story. But verse 17 says Hadad fled to Egypt with his father's servants. Moab shows up later in this passage as the home of the god Chemosh, so it's in the neighborhood of the story. The road for Hadad's group ran through Midian and Paran, and it ended in Egypt (1 Kings 11:18).

Assyria doesn't appear anywhere in this passage. Verse 17 says Hadad fled to Egypt, along with some Edomites who were servants of his father. That's a long way from Assyria on any map. Egypt is where the story takes him.

explanations.answer: A house and land and food
explanations.explanation: That's the whole package. Verse 18 says Pharaoh “gave Hadad a house and land and provided him with food.” Pharaoh is the king of Egypt. Hadad shows up as a refugee, and he gets a roof, a field and meals, which is a pretty strong welcome.

explanations.answer: A post in his royal army
explanations.explanation: Pharaoh does make Hadad comfortable, but no army post is in the text. Verse 18 says Pharaoh gave him a house and land and provided him with food. Pharaoh is the king of Egypt, and he was looking after Hadad, not recruiting him. The army isn't in the picture.

explanations.answer: A ship to sail back home
explanations.explanation: No ship in this one, friend. Verse 18 says Pharaoh gave Hadad a house and land and provided him with food. The text doesn't send Hadad home until he asks to go, years later (1 Kings 11:21). Pharaoh, king of Egypt, gave him something to settle into first.

True. Verse 20 says Genubath was weaned in Pharaoh's palace by Queen Tahpenes herself, and that he “lived there among the sons of Pharaoh.” Pharaoh is the king of Egypt, and Genubath is Hadad's son. So Hadad's boy grew up with the royal kids.

The text says the opposite. Verse 20 says Genubath, Hadad's son, was weaned in Pharaoh's palace by Queen Tahpenes herself, and that he “lived there among the sons of Pharaoh.” Pharaoh is the king of Egypt. So the palace was Genubath's home, and this statement is true.

explanations.answer: To let him return to his own country
explanations.explanation: Right. Hadad hears that David, Israel's old king, has rested with his fathers and that Joab, the commander of the army, is dead. Then he says to Pharaoh, “Let me go, that I may return to my own country.” (1 Kings 11:21) Both of the men connected to Edom's tragedy are gone, and Hadad speaks up.

explanations.answer: To give him soldiers to fight Israel
explanations.explanation: Soldiers aren't in his request. Verse 21 gives Hadad's words to Pharaoh: “Let me go, that I may return to my own country.” He asks to go home, and that's all he asks. David and Joab are both gone by then, but the text puts no war plan in his mouth.

explanations.answer: To let Genubath rule over Edom
explanations.explanation: The text never mentions Genubath ruling anything. Hadad's request in verse 21 is short: “Let me go, that I may return to my own country.” Genubath is Hadad's son, who lived in Pharaoh's palace. Hadad asks for himself, and nothing is said about his boy's future.

explanations.answer: He lacked nothing but still wants to go
explanations.explanation: That's what Hadad says. Pharaoh asks what he has lacked, and Hadad answers, “Nothing,” … “but please let me go.” (1 Kings 11:22) No complaint, no list, no explanation. The text leaves it there, and so do I.

explanations.answer: He misses his father's people in Edom
explanations.explanation: It sounds natural, but Hadad doesn't say it. Pharaoh asks what he has lacked, and Hadad answers, “Nothing,” … “but please let me go.” (1 Kings 11:22) The text gives no reason beyond that. I think a lot was going through his head, but that's my guess, not his words.

explanations.answer: He fears Pharaoh will turn against him
explanations.explanation: Hadad never says that. Pharaoh asks what he has lacked, and Hadad answers, “Nothing,” … “but please let me go.” (1 Kings 11:22) Earlier, the text said he found such great favor with Pharaoh (1 Kings 11:19). So the text shows no fear, just a short answer and a request.

Master is the word. Rezon, son of Eliada, “had fled from his master, Hadadezer king of Zobah.” (1 Kings 11:23) Notice Rezon runs from the man he served, and then he gathers men of his own. So the second adversary is a runaway servant, not a rival king.

The text says nothing about a brother. Rezon, son of Eliada, “had fled from his master, Hadadezer king of Zobah.” (1 Kings 11:23) Hadadezer was the king Rezon served. Rezon walked out on his boss, and then he built his own crew.

An ally would be a friend, and verse 23 gives a different word. Rezon, son of Eliada, “had fled from his master, Hadadezer king of Zobah.” (1 Kings 11:23) A servant who flees his master is running away, not standing beside him. Master is the one.

Damascus it is. After David killed the Zobaites, Rezon captained a band of raiders and “went to Damascus, where they settled and gained control.” (1 Kings 11:24) A crew of raiders ended up running the town. That's how a runaway servant becomes a ruler over Aram (1 Kings 11:25).

Hebron is a real place, but it isn't in this story. Rezon's band of raiders “went to Damascus, where they settled and gained control.” (1 Kings 11:24) They didn't just pass through. They moved in and took charge.

Gath doesn't show up in this passage. The text says Rezon's band of raiders “went to Damascus, where they settled and gained control.” (1 Kings 11:24) Settled and gained control is a big step up from raiding. Damascus is the answer.

It's the other way around, friend. Verse 25 says, “Rezon was Israel’s enemy throughout the days of Solomon, adding to the trouble caused by Hadad.” Rezon ruled over Aram with hostility toward Israel. Peace never gets a mention.

False is right. Verse 25 says, “Rezon was Israel’s enemy throughout the days of Solomon, adding to the trouble caused by Hadad.” He ruled over Aram with hostility toward Israel. Solomon, David's son and Israel's king, had a neighbor who stayed against him the whole time.

True. Verse 26 says, “Jeroboam was a servant of Solomon, but he rebelled against the king.” Jeroboam son of Nebat is an Ephraimite from Zeredah, and his mother is a widow named Zeruah. So this trouble comes from inside Solomon's own house.

The text says he was. Verse 26 says, “Jeroboam was a servant of Solomon, but he rebelled against the king.” Jeroboam son of Nebat, an Ephraimite from Zeredah, worked for Solomon, David's son and Israel's king. That's what makes this one different from Hadad and Rezon, who came from outside.

explanations.answer: Puts him over the labor force of Joseph's house
explanations.explanation: Yes. Solomon, Israel's king, noticed that the young man was industrious, so “he put him in charge of the whole labor force of the house of Joseph.” (1 Kings 11:28) Jeroboam is called a mighty man of valor, and his work got noticed. A big promotion, and the text goes on to call it Jeroboam's rebellion account.

explanations.answer: Makes him commander of the whole army
explanations.explanation: The army isn't in his job description. Solomon noticed the young man was industrious and “put him in charge of the whole labor force of the house of Joseph.” (1 Kings 11:28) That's a workforce, not a battle line. Jeroboam was called a mighty man of valor, but the text gives him labor to oversee.

explanations.answer: Sends him to rebuild the walls of Gezer
explanations.explanation: Gezer doesn't come up here. Verse 28 says Solomon “put him in charge of the whole labor force of the house of Joseph.” The text does mention Solomon building supporting terraces and repairing a gap in the wall of the city of his father David (1 Kings 11:27). But that's Jerusalem, and Jeroboam is the one in charge of the workers.

That's what he does. Ahijah the Shilonite, a prophet, “took hold of the new cloak he was wearing, tore it into twelve pieces,” (1 Kings 11:30). It's just the two of them alone in the open field. A brand new cloak ripped to shreds, and it's a message from the LORD.

No gift of a coat here. Ahijah the Shilonite, a prophet, took hold of the new cloak he was wearing and “tore it into twelve pieces,” (1 Kings 11:30). Then he hands Jeroboam some of the pieces (1 Kings 11:31). So Jeroboam gets pieces, not a cloak to wear.

explanations.answer: Spreads it out on the road
explanations.explanation: The cloak never gets laid down. Ahijah the Shilonite, a prophet, took hold of the new cloak he was wearing and “tore it into twelve pieces,” (1 Kings 11:30). Then he speaks for the LORD to Jeroboam. The cloak ends up in pieces, not on the ground.

Tribes is right. Ahijah says the LORD will tear the kingdom out of the hand of Solomon, “and I will give you ten tribes.” (1 Kings 11:31) Ten pieces of cloak, ten tribes of Israel. The cloak was the picture, and the words explain it.

The word is bigger than cities. Ahijah says, “Behold, I will tear the kingdom out of the hand of Solomon, and I will give you ten tribes.” (1 Kings 11:31) Each cloak piece lines up with a tribe. The people are what get divided, not a list of towns.

Armies don't come up in this promise. Ahijah says the LORD will tear the kingdom out of Solomon's hand, “and I will give you ten tribes.” (1 Kings 11:31) The ten pieces of cloak stand for ten tribes. No soldiers, just a torn kingdom.

explanations.answer: For the sake of David and Jerusalem
explanations.explanation: Right. The LORD says, “But one tribe will remain for the sake of My servant David and for the sake of Jerusalem, the city I have chosen out of all the tribes of Israel.” (1 Kings 11:32) David is Israel's earlier king, and Jerusalem is where the LORD chose to put His Name (1 Kings 11:36). Two reasons are named, so we keep it to those two.

explanations.answer: Because Solomon will turn back to Him
explanations.explanation: The LORD doesn't say that. He says one tribe will remain “for the sake of My servant David and for the sake of Jerusalem, the city I have chosen out of all the tribes of Israel.” (1 Kings 11:32) Solomon turning back isn't in the promise. The reasons are David and Jerusalem.

explanations.answer: Because Jeroboam will ask for mercy
explanations.explanation: Jeroboam isn't asking for anything in this scene. The LORD says one tribe will remain “for the sake of My servant David and for the sake of Jerusalem, the city I have chosen out of all the tribes of Israel.” (1 Kings 11:32) Jeroboam is only listening to Ahijah, a prophet. The reasons the LORD gives are David and Jerusalem.

explanations.answer: Forsaking Him to worship other gods
explanations.explanation: That's the reason the LORD gives. “For they have forsaken Me to worship Ashtoreth the goddess of the Sidonians, Chemosh the god of the Moabites, and Milcom the god of the Ammonites.” (1 Kings 11:33) These are false gods of neighboring nations. The LORD is telling Jeroboam why the kingdom is being torn.

The wall isn't the reason. The text mentions Solomon repairing the gap in the wall of the city of David (1 Kings 11:27), but that's a separate detail. The LORD says, “For they have forsaken Me to worship Ashtoreth the goddess of the Sidonians, Chemosh the god of the Moabites, and Milcom the god of the Ammonites.” (1 Kings 11:33) The reason is worshiping other gods.

No treaty is named by the LORD here. He says, “For they have forsaken Me to worship Ashtoreth the goddess of the Sidonians, Chemosh the god of the Moabites, and Milcom the god of the Ammonites.” (1 Kings 11:33) Pharaoh, king of Egypt, shows up in this passage with Hadad and later with Jeroboam. But the reason for the torn kingdom is the worship of other gods.

explanations.answer: All the days of his life
explanations.explanation: Yes. The LORD says, “Nevertheless, I will not take the whole kingdom out of Solomon’s hand, because I have made him ruler all the days of his life for the sake of David My servant…” (1 Kings 11:34) Solomon, Israel's king, stays on the throne for his whole life. The tearing comes later.

Jeroboam is already a young man in this scene, and the LORD doesn't tie Solomon's rule to his age. He says, “I will not take the whole kingdom out of Solomon’s hand, because I have made him ruler all the days of his life for the sake of David My servant…” (1 Kings 11:34) Solomon, Israel's king, rules his whole life. No age gets mentioned.

No number of years is given. The LORD says, “I will not take the whole kingdom out of Solomon’s hand, because I have made him ruler all the days of his life for the sake of David My servant…” (1 Kings 11:34) That means for his whole life. I'd hold off on counting years.

Son is right. The LORD says, “But I will take ten tribes of the kingdom from the hand of his son and give them to you.” (1 Kings 11:35) So Solomon keeps the whole kingdom in his lifetime, and the tearing falls on his son. The text names that son at the end of the passage (1 Kings 11:43).

No steward in this one. The LORD says, “But I will take ten tribes of the kingdom from the hand of his son and give them to you.” (1 Kings 11:35) Solomon, Israel's king, has a son who will rule after him. That's whose hand the tribes come out of.

A captain isn't mentioned here. The LORD says, “But I will take ten tribes of the kingdom from the hand of his son and give them to you.” (1 Kings 11:35) The tribes come from the hand of Solomon's son, the next king after Solomon. It's a family matter at the throne, not a military one.

explanations.answer: He will be king over Israel
explanations.explanation: That's the promise. The LORD says, “But as for you, I will take you, and you shall reign over all that your heart desires, and you will be king over Israel.” (1 Kings 11:37) Jeroboam, once a servant of Solomon, hears he will be a king. I bet that field got very quiet.

explanations.answer: He will be a prophet like Ahijah
explanations.explanation: Ahijah the Shilonite is the prophet here, and Jeroboam isn't told to be one. The LORD says, “But as for you, I will take you, and you shall reign over all that your heart desires, and you will be king over Israel.” (1 Kings 11:37) Jeroboam is promised a throne. Prophets and kings are different jobs.

explanations.answer: He will be governor over Ephraim
explanations.explanation: Ephraim is Jeroboam's tribe, but the promise is bigger than that. The LORD says, “But as for you, I will take you, and you shall reign over all that your heart desires, and you will be king over Israel.” (1 Kings 11:37) A king over Israel, not a governor over one tribe. That's a much larger job.

Dynasty is right. The LORD says, “If you listen to all that I command you, walk in My ways, and do what is right in My sight in order to keep My statutes and commandments as My servant David did, then I will be with you. I will build you a lasting dynasty just as I built for David, and I will give Israel to you.” (1 Kings 11:38) The promise comes with an if. Listening comes first.

The LORD doesn't promise Jeroboam a temple. He says, “I will build you a lasting dynasty just as I built for David, and I will give Israel to you.” (1 Kings 11:38) A dynasty is a line of kings that keeps going. And it all depends on Jeroboam listening to what the LORD commands.

A palace is a building, and the promise is bigger than a building. The LORD says, “I will build you a lasting dynasty just as I built for David, and I will give Israel to you.” (1 Kings 11:38) A dynasty is a lasting line of kings. And it comes with the if of obeying all that He commands.

Not quite, friend. The LORD says, “Because of this, I will humble David’s descendants…” and then He adds that it is not forever (1 Kings 11:39). David's family gets humbled, and that is not the last word. So the statement is false.

False is right. The LORD tells Jeroboam that He will humble David's descendants, but not forever (1 Kings 11:39). The humbling has an end. That fits with the lamp the LORD promised David in Jerusalem (1 Kings 11:36).

explanations.answer: He flees to Shishak king of Egypt
explanations.explanation: That's what Jeroboam does. Verse 40 says, “Solomon therefore sought to kill Jeroboam. But Jeroboam arose and fled to Egypt, to Shishak king of Egypt, where he remained until the death of Solomon.” Solomon is Israel's king, and Jeroboam is the servant he's after. Egypt is also where young Hadad fled earlier in this passage.

explanations.answer: He hides in the hill country of Ephraim
explanations.explanation: Ephraim is Jeroboam's home tribe, but that's not where he goes. Verse 40 says, “But Jeroboam arose and fled to Egypt, to Shishak king of Egypt…” Solomon, Israel's king, was looking to kill him. So he left the country.

explanations.answer: He raises an army against Solomon
explanations.explanation: No army in this part of the story. Verse 40 says Solomon sought to kill Jeroboam, and “Jeroboam arose and fled to Egypt, to Shishak king of Egypt…” Solomon is Israel's king. Jeroboam ran, and he stayed away for a good while.

Yes. Jeroboam fled to Shishak king of Egypt, “where he remained until the death of Solomon.” (1 Kings 11:40) He stays tucked away until Solomon, Israel's king, is gone. The text sets his waiting by Solomon's life, not by a number.

Hadad never sends for anyone in this passage. Verse 40 says Jeroboam fled to Egypt and stayed “until the death of Solomon.” Hadad is the Edomite who also found a home in Egypt earlier. The clock that matters for Jeroboam is Solomon's life.

The text doesn't give a count of years. Verse 40 says Jeroboam stayed in Egypt with Shishak, its king, “until the death of Solomon.” That could be a short stay or a long one, and I'd rather not guess. The marker is Solomon's death.

That's the one. Verse 43 says Solomon “rested with his fathers and was buried in the city of his father David. And his son Rehoboam reigned in his place.” Solomon reigned forty years over all Israel (1 Kings 11:42). Rehoboam is the son the LORD's words pointed to (1 Kings 11:35).

Jeroboam has the promise, but he isn't the next king yet. Verse 43 says Solomon “rested with his fathers and was buried in the city of his father David. And his son Rehoboam reigned in his place.” Jeroboam is still in Egypt when Solomon dies (1 Kings 11:40). The throne goes to Solomon's son first.

Hadad was one of Solomon's adversaries, so he never takes the throne in Jerusalem. Verse 43 says Solomon “rested with his fathers and was buried in the city of his father David. And his son Rehoboam reigned in his place.” The new king is Solomon's own son. That's the fact the text hands us.
